name: Daniel Gross
milestone_by_age_26: In 2010, at about age 18–19, accepted as the then-youngest Y Combinator founder (W10) and co-founded Greplin (later Cue); by ~19 raised Sequoia capital and by 2013 (age ~22) sold Cue to Apple for a reported $40–60M.
early_history_summary: Born in Jerusalem in 1991 and raised in an Orthodox Jewish environment, Gross expected a traditional religious path in Israel. While in mechina before IDF enlistment he applied to Y Combinator on a whim, became its youngest founder at the time, and built Greplin into a predictive personal-search product that Sequoia backed and Apple acquired.
family_context_summary: Born in Jerusalem; raised in an Orthodox Jewish family context and planned a traditional religious life in Israel before pivoting via YC.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Y Combinator, Sequoia, Silicon Valley, youngest YC founder, Apple acquisition
evidence_summary: Gross left a traditional Israeli religious track to join YC W10 as its youngest founder, shipping Greplin/Cue and raising Sequoia at ~19 before an Apple acquisition at ~22. He later ran AI/search work at Apple, partnered at YC (launching YC AI), co-invested heavily in AI with Nat Friedman, co-founded Safe Superintelligence with Ilya Sutskever, and in 2025 joined Meta Superintelligence Labs. Early advantage centers on YC/Sequoia institutional acceleration and Silicon Valley immersion rather than documented family capital or domain inheritance.
starting_point: Born 1991 in Jerusalem; raised Orthodox Jewish with an expected traditional religious life in Israel before applying to Y Combinator.
current_position: Technology investor and AI executive; left Safe Superintelligence Inc. (co-founded 2024 with Ilya Sutskever) to join Meta Superintelligence Labs in 2025; previously YC partner and Apple AI lead.

trajectory.event: Accepted to Y Combinator W10 as then-youngest founder and co-founded Greplin (later Cue) for unified personal search.
Raised ~$4M from Sequoia Capital for Greplin and was named to Forbes 30 Under 30 in technology.
Apple acquired Cue for a reported $40–60M; Gross joined Apple to lead machine-learning/search efforts.
Left Apple to become a Y Combinator partner and launched YC’s dedicated AI track.
Founded Pioneer, a global remote early-stage talent accelerator and fund.
With Nat Friedman, deployed the Andromeda GPU cluster for portfolio AI startups; named to TIME100 AI.
Co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc. with Ilya Sutskever and Daniel Levy.
Left SSI to join Meta Superintelligence Labs working on AI products.

early_history_summary: Marsha J. Berger earned a B.S. in mathematics from SUNY Binghamton in 1974, worked as a scientific programmer at Argonne National Laboratory, then completed an M.S. (1978) and Ph.D. (1982) in computer science at Stanford before joining NYU’s Courant Institute.
evidence_summary: Berger’s documented breakthrough work—adaptive mesh refinement for hyperbolic PDEs and later Cart3D—came with and after her 1982 Stanford Ph.D. (age ~29). Recognition such as NAS (2000), NAE (2005), and major prizes followed mid-career. Education and Argonne programming by 26 do not constitute a material breakout milestone under the strict ≤26 rule.

name: Alec Muffett
milestone_by_age_26: In 1990–1991, at age 22–23 while a Unix systems programmer at the University of Wales Aberystwyth, created and publicly released Crack (first public Usenet release v2.7a on 15 July 1991)—the first widely used standalone Unix password cracker, later foundational for admin security tooling and CrackLib.
early_history_summary: Born 22 April 1968, Muffett graduated in astronomy from UCL (1988) then worked as a systems programmer at UCW Aberystwyth (1988–1991). There he rewrote Dan Farmer’s pwc into Crack, releasing it publicly in 1991 before joining Sun Microsystems in 1992 and rising to principal security engineer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Unix admin immersion, Usenet release, password security, university systems role
evidence_summary: Muffett’s breakout was building Crack as a working systems programmer in his early twenties—directly solving weak-password problems on university Unix hosts and releasing via Usenet. The tool became the first standalone Unix password cracker and influenced John the Ripper’s rule syntax; he later spent ~17 years at Sun and helped launch Tor onion services for major news sites. Family advantage is undocumented; leverage came from hands-on admin exposure and early open distribution.
starting_point: Born 22 April 1968 (Anglo-American background); educated in astronomy at UCL before entering university systems programming in Wales.
current_position: Independent internet-security technologist, consultant, and writer; known for Crack/CrackLib work and later Tor onion service deployments for major publishers.

trajectory.event: Graduated UCL in astronomy and began systems programming at University of Wales Aberystwyth.
Began developing Crack by rewriting and extending Dan Farmer’s pwc password checker for campus Unix security.
Publicly released Crack v2.7a on Usenet (15 July 1991); later 1991 releases added programmable dictionary rules and network cracking.
Joined Sun Microsystems, later becoming principal engineer for security until 2009.
Participated in research factoring RSA-155 (512-bit RSA challenge number).
Named among SC Magazine’s top influential security thinkers.
Helped bring The New York Times and other major sites online as Tor onion services.

name: Walter Bright
milestone_by_age_26: Around 1977–1978, at about age 18 while a student at Caltech, designed and implemented Empire, an early full-featured computer strategy wargame on the PDP-10 that spread widely (later DECUS distribution) and became a foundational 4X/empire-building computer game lineage.
early_history_summary: Born 10 March 1959, son of USAF pilot Charles D. Bright, Walter taught himself programming from type-in BASIC games, entered Caltech, and built Empire in FORTRAN after learning the language for the project. He graduated Caltech in 1979 (mechanical engineering) and later created Zortech C++ and the D programming language.
family_context_summary: Son of United States Air Force pilot Charles D. Bright; taught himself programming from published BASIC listings.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a military pilot/aerospace figure (not a software engineer); limited evidence of direct software-domain transfer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Caltech, PDP-10 free student time, Empire game, early compilers
evidence_summary: Bright’s first material, dated achievement was shipping Empire as a Caltech undergrad on scarce mainframe time, with peer mentoring from friends who taught him programming. He later commercialized Empire, built the first native C++ compiler (Zortech), and created the D language. Early advantages are Caltech access, mainframe facilities, and self-driven compiler depth rather than family software capital.
starting_point: Born 10 March 1959 to a U.S. Air Force pilot father; self-taught programming via BASIC game listings before Caltech.
current_position: Creator of the D programming language and Digital Mars tools; continues compiler and language work; living American programmer known for Empire, Zortech C++, and D.

trajectory.event: Wrote Empire, a pioneering PDP-10 strategy wargame at Caltech that became widely played and later redistributed.
Graduated Caltech with a B.S. in mechanical engineering (aeronautical minor); had also written Intellivision games while a student.
Announced PDP-11 Empire in BYTE; later reclaimed authorship credit with DECUS for redistributed Empire sources.
Interstel published Empire: Wargame of the Century commercially to strong market success.
Developed Zortech C++, widely cited as the first C++ compiler to compile directly to object code without a C intermediate.
Released the first version of the D programming language (Digital Mars D).
Wrote Warp, a high-performance C/C++ preprocessor in D for Facebook, open-sourced the same year.
